title: Preparing SALNs
primary_topics: Practical guide to filling out the SALN form -- prompted by the Corona impeachment trial questions about declaration requirements
The proper value to declare for real properties: acquisition cost (not market or assessed value) as the anti-graft law benchmark
The legal consequences of incomplete, inaccurate, or untruthful SALN declarations -- administrative, criminal, and civil sanctions
sub_topics: April 30, 2012 deadline for all public officials and employees to file SALNs -- required by Constitution, Anti-Graft Law (RA 3019) and Ethical Standards Law (RA 6713)
SALN form prescribed by the Civil Service Commission (CSC) since 1994: two-page, back-to-back
Three real estate values required: assessed value, current fair market value, and acquisition cost
Republic v. Sandiganbayan (Jan. 30, 2002, CJ Davide): acquisition cost, not market or assessed value, is used in computing ill-gotten wealth under RA 1379
Acquisition cost: amount stated in deed of sale; improvement costs require honest, educated good-faith estimate
Assessed and market values: city/provincial assessors assessment acceptable; honest errors in approximation should not constitute SALN falsification
Personal and other properties: three columns (kind, year acquired, acquisition cost) from invoices and receipts
Motor vehicles must be declared: Flores v. Montemayor (June 8, 2011) -- employee dismissed for omitting two expensive cars
Business interests and financial connections (backside): Rabe v. Flores (May 14, 1997) -- employee dismissed with forfeiture for failing to disclose a market stall
Ombudsman v. Valeroso (Apr. 2, 2007): SALN requires true, detailed and sworn declaration; valid check and balance mechanism to verify undisclosed properties

Consequences of failure: administrative (reprimand, fine, suspension, dismissal, forfeiture, permanent ban); criminal (perjury, falsification, RA 3019/RA 6713 -- imprisonment or fine); civil (forfeiture of manifestly disproportionate properties)
OMB constitutional mandate and RA 6770 to investigate and initiate recovery of ill-gotten wealth; for impeachable officials, may file verified impeachment complaint

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes on the eve of the April 30, 2012 SALN filing deadline for all public officials and employees, providing a practical guide to filling out the two-page Civil Service Commission form -- prompted by the Corona impeachment trial's public education effect on SALN requirements. He clarifies the most contested issue: the SALN form requires three real estate values (assessed, current fair market, and acquisition cost), but acquisition cost -- not market or assessed value -- is the legally correct basis for determining whether a public official has amassed ill-gotten wealth, as held by the SC in Republic v. Sandiganbayan (January 30, 2002, CJ Davide). Acquisition cost is the amount in the deed of sale; improvement costs require an honest good-faith estimate; honest errors in approximating market values should not constitute falsification. For personal properties, invoices and receipts provide the data; motor vehicles must be declared (Flores v. Montemayor, 2011 -- dismissal for omitting two cars). Business interests and financial connections must also be declared (Rabe v. Flores, 1997 -- dismissal for failing to disclose a market stall). The SC in Ombudsman v. Valeroso (2007) described the SALN as 'a valid check and balance mechanism to verify undisclosed properties and wealth.' Failure to file complete, accurate, and truthful SALNs may subject the declarant to administrative sanctions (reprimand to dismissal plus forfeiture and permanent ban), criminal liability, and civil forfeiture of properties manifestly disproportionate to legitimate income -- all enforced primarily by the OMB.
